newsitem.title: USA: Clinton approves U.S. troops for Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Clinton approves U.S. troops for Zaire.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Wednesday tentatively agreed to order U.S. troops to help in an international rescue of some one million refugees in eastern Zaire and the Pentagon said the troops could go next week.

White House Press Secretary Mike McCurry said the U.S. commitment, expected to last about four months, involves sending 1,000 ground troops to the African nation. An additional 2,000 to 3,000 American troops would go to nearby countries to help with support activities, the Pentagon said.

"The president has decided that the United States is willing, in principle, to participate in a limited fashion in this mission as long as certain conditions are stipulated to," McCurry said at a White House briefing.
Among the conditions he listed were that the mission would be of limited duration and made up of a multinational force.

Canadian Army Lt. Gen. Maurice Baril will lead the multilateral force to bring in aid to desperate Rwandan and Burundian Hutus, some cut off from help since local Tutsis rebelled a month ago. British and French troops would also take part.

"(U.S.) troops could be flowing into place sometime next week," said a senior Pentagon official, adding that the 1,000 troops in Zaire would include about 600 elite paratroopers from the U.S. 508th Airborne Infantry Regiment based at Vicenza, Italy.
The White House announcement cleared the way for the U.N. Security Council to work on a resolution, already drafted by Canada, in hopes it can be adopted by the end of the week.
White House National Security Adviser and Defence Undersecretary Walter Slocombe will go to the United Nations (on) Thursday to discuss the matter, a senior Pentagon official told reporters.
McCurry also said the mission would have to be "very clearly defined" and it would not try to disarm militants or conduct any kind of "forced entry."

Defence Secretary William Perry told reporters the United States planned to send about 1,000 troops to the eastern Zaire town of Goma to secure and run the airport, the key centre for distributing relief.
They will also set up a protected corridor about 2 miles (3 km) long from Goma to nearby Rwanda to allow refugees to return to Rwanda if the voluntarily chose to do so, the Pentagon said.

Defence officials said other U.S. troops in the task force were expected to include air cargo handlers and medical, civil affairs and "psychological operations" personnel, who would encourage refugees to voluntarily return to Rwanda.

U.S. officials said although the multinational force would be under the overall command of a Canadian general, the U.S. forces would directly serve under an American general who will serve as deputy commander.

Perry stressed the U.S. decision to participate in the force was contingent on securing commitments from African countries involved, principally Zaire and Rwanda, not to interfere with the mission. "Our assumption is that we would have their acquiesence," he said.

In addition, Perry said there would be discussions in coming days with other countries involved on a number of other issues, including a clear definition of the mission, an exit strategy and the command structure.
A 40-member U.S. military team was in Uganda on Wednesday and also travelled to Rwanda. It was expected to go to Zaire later in the week.

Despite a broad consensus that the Zaire crisis could lead to thousands of deaths without urgent action, Clinton -- re-elected last week to a second term -- and other officials have approached the matter with reluctance and caution.
The United States has painful memories of a U.N. relief mission to Somalia in 1993, which led to heavy casualties among U.S. and other troops.
Clinton discussed Zaire's refugee crisis with other world leaders, including Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien, by telephone on Wednesday.
